questions.q: What is the protagonist of the poem "The Peacock," and how is it introduced in the first three lines?
questions.a: The protagonist is the peacock, introduced through its "loud sharp call" that "seems to come from nowhere" followed by "a flash of turquoise / in the pipal tree" — establishing it as auditory and visual but spatially ambiguous. A wrong answer (e.g., "the speaker" or "the cat") reveals the student confuses the observer with the observed, or focuses on minor elements instead of the central figure the poem is named after and consistently describes.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the speaker is told to "sit in the veranda / And read a book... with great concentration" in order to see the peacock.
questions.a: The instruction creates a paradox: the peacock appears only when the speaker is *not* looking for it — deep absorption in a book makes the observer still and unaware, which allows the elusive bird to reveal itself. A wrong answer (e.g., "to pass time" or "because the speaker likes reading") shows the student misses the strategic irony: the peacock's character is defined by its avoidance of direct attention, so the speaker must *feign* inattention to witness it.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "show, don't tell" to analyze how the poet reveals the peacock's personality through its movements in lines 4–8 ("The slender neck arched away from you / as he descends, / and as he darts away, a glimpse / of the very end of his tail").
questions.a: The verbs "arched away," "descends," "darts away," and the phrase "glimpse / of the very end of his tail" show a creature that is graceful but deliberate in its withdrawal — it controls the encounter, offering only fragments. The movement is never toward the speaker, always away. A wrong answer listing only "it moves beautifully" misses the directional intentionality: each verb choice reinforces the peacock's autonomy and reluctance to be fully seen.

questions.q: Analyze how the natural world (wind, bees, cat) reacts to the peacock's presence, and what this suggests about the peacock's status in the poem's ecosystem.
questions.a: The wind changes direction, the bees' hum stops, the cat awakens and stretches — all ordinary rhythms break at the peacock's arrival. This positions the peacock as a disruptive, almost supernatural presence that commands the environment's attention without effort. A wrong answer treating these as random details fails to see the pathetic fallacy: nature itself pauses, signaling the peacock's symbolic weight as a moment of epiphany.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the final two lines ("It is the tail that has to blink / For eyes that are always open") as a characterization of the peacock. Does this metaphor deepen or confuse the protagonist's portrayal?
questions.a: The metaphor deepens the portrayal by reversing expectations: the tail's "eyes" (ocelli) blink when the tail closes, while the real eyes never close — suggesting the peacock is eternally vigilant, and its beauty is a defense mechanism. The bird sees everything but reveals little. A wrong answer calling it "just a description of feathers" ignores the personification and thematic resonance: the protagonist is defined by watchful withdrawal, not display.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza in free verse that captures the same elusive, color-rich character of the peacock but from the *peacock's own perspective* — using first person and at least two colors from the poem.
questions.a:
A strong response might read:  
"I fold my violet-fringed amber eyes / And vanish into pipal shade — / Turquoise is a secret I keep / Until the wind forgets my name."  
This uses first person, includes "violet," "amber," "turquoise," and conveys deliberate concealment. A weak answer describes the bird from outside (third person) or uses no color imagery, showing the student hasn't internalized the protagonist's voice or visual palette.
